addressed_problems.content: It remains to be investigated whether exponential interaction models, arising as the $p\to\infty$ limit of the $p$-body dense Hopfield networks studied in Chapter 2, can achieve $\mathcal{O}(N)$ noise tolerance when the teacher-student setting is considered, even though such tolerance would come at the cost of an exponential number of training examples. This question is motivated by the analysis of dense Hopfield networks with $p\geq 3$, which already exhibit $\mathcal{O}(N^{1-2/p})$ noise tolerance, and the expectation that the $p\to\infty$ limit may saturate at $\mathcal{O}(N)$ tolerance. Resolving this would clarify the fundamental limits of noise resilience in high-capacity associative memory models.

For the dense associative memory model of Chapter 4, further research is needed to determine the asymptotic functional form of the training time when using the splitting steepest descent algorithm. The empirical results suggest a logarithmic scaling with the number of hidden units, but a rigorous characterization is still lacking and would be important for understanding the algorithm's efficiency in large-scale applications.

It is also interesting to study the teacher-student setting of the dense associative memory model of Chapter 4 when the teacher inverse temperature $\beta^*$ is less than order $N$ (i.e., when the teacher generates data with a finite noise level). This would extend the current analysis, which assumed $\beta^*/N$ fixed, and could reveal new regimes of learnability and optimal regularization strategies.

The tradeoff between the splitting steepest descent algorithm (used in Chapter 4) and methods that break permutation symmetry by adding random noise should be investigated. While splitting steepest descent finds the fastest escape directions from saddle points, it is computationally more expensive than random perturbation. Identifying the regimes where each method is preferable would guide practical implementations of network-growing algorithms.

More generally, one could study how permutation symmetry breaking takes place in energy models related to the dense associative memory of Chapter 4, such as attentional Boltzmann machines. Understanding the dynamics of symmetry breaking in these models could reveal universal principles that govern the learning of structured representations and could be exploited to improve training.

An intriguing open question is whether there are similarities between cellular division and the splitting steepest descent algorithm used to train dense associative memories in Chapter 4. If such connections exist, they could provide a biological metaphor for the network-growing dynamics and inspire new algorithms inspired by developmental processes.

Finally, it would be interesting to see if the splitting steepest descent algorithm and the regularization technique proposed in Chapter 4 (based on the effective loss with a regularizing parameter $\varsigma$) can improve the training of transformers and generative diffusion models. Given the connections between modern Hopfield networks and attention mechanisms, these techniques might offer practical benefits for widely used architectures.

It would be interesting to study exponential models of dense Hopfield networks (i.e., the $p\to\infty$ limit of the $p$-body models) in the teacher-student setting, complementing existing studies of the direct model. This would extend the analysis of Chapter 2 to a regime where the storage capacity and retrieval properties are qualitatively different, and could provide new insights into the interplay between model complexity, noise tolerance, and learning performance.

An open problem is to extend the adversarial attack analysis of dense Hopfield networks from a teacher with a single pattern to a teacher with at least two patterns, which would allow a more complete description of attacks aiming to misclassify data. This could be tackled using an approach similar to that used for restricted Boltzmann machines with multiple hidden units in Chapter 3, and would help clarify whether the adversarial robustness mechanisms identified in the single-pattern case carry over to multi-class settings.

It remains to be investigated whether the independence of learning performance on the number of hidden units, observed in restricted Boltzmann machines with uncorrelated teacher patterns in Chapter 3, also holds for $p$-body dense networks. This would generalize the permutation symmetry breaking results of Chapter 3 to higher-order interaction models and test the universality of the factorization property that underlies the independence.

For the restricted Boltzmann machine model studied in Chapter 3, one could study the learning dynamics of the magnitude pruning experiment (used to identify winning lottery tickets) to gain additional insight into the lottery ticket hypothesis. This would involve analyzing how the convergence speed of the winning ticket depends on the initial conditions and the training dynamics, and could reveal common properties of fortuitous initializations that lead to faster training.

A further unresolved issue is to characterize the distribution of winning ticket initial conditions in the restricted Boltzmann machine teacher-student setting of Chapter 3. Understanding the statistical properties of the subnetworks that converge quickly could provide a theoretical foundation for the lottery ticket hypothesis and guide the design of novel initialization schemes.

It would be valuable to extend the restricted Boltzmann machine analysis of Chapter 3 to the case where the number of hidden units $P$ and the number of teacher patterns $P^*$ are of order $N$ (the input dimension), rather than finite. This is relevant because real-world RBMs typically have a large number of hidden units, and the current finite-$P$ results may not capture the scaling behavior and phase transitions that occur in that regime.

An interesting direction is to introduce correlations between the columns of the teacher's weight matrix in the restricted Boltzmann machine (i.e., a low-rank SVD structure) in addition to the correlations between patterns studied in Chapter 3. This would allow the teacher to generate data with even more structure, and could be used to investigate whether the distinct permutation symmetry breaking phases ($\text{PSB}_s$ and $\text{PSB}_t$) persist in real data and have a measurable effect on the critical slowing down observed in RBM training.

Beyond the specific restricted Boltzmann machine model of Chapter 3, it would be worthwhile to study other generative models with a finite number of hidden units in the teacher-student setting, such as modern Hopfield networks (dense associative memories). This would test the generality of the factorization property and the permutation symmetry breaking transitions observed in RBMs, and could reveal new phenomena unique to high-capacity models.

Artificial neural networks (NNs) and machine learning (ML) algorithms are poorly understood from a theoretical perspective, which makes it difficult to fully realize their potential and overcome their weaknesses. Two key unresolved issues motivate this thesis. First, ML algorithms train NN weights by moving them along a low-dimensional subspace of their allowed values, but this implicitly low-dimensional learning structure is not properly exploited to improve training because its nature is not well understood. Second, trained NNs are easily confused by pervasive adversarial attacks whose theoretical underpinnings are still unclear. This thesis aims to improve our theoretical understanding of NNs and ML, with a particular focus on adversarial attacks and implicitly low-dimensional learning, using mathematical tools from statistical mechanics. The work studies two classes of models that fit data with various degrees of learning and memorization: dense associative memory (DAM) and restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM). In the process, it investigates connections between different versions of these models that are useful to make analytical investigations more efficient. Specifically, the thesis addresses: (i) the relationship between the direct problem (random pattern retrieval) and the inverse problem (teacher-student learning) in dense Hopfield networks, and the implications for adversarial robustness; (ii) the effects of data correlations and number of hidden units on RBM learning in the teacher-student setting, including a toy model of the lottery ticket hypothesis; (iii) the stationary points of a DAM model capable of supervised and unsupervised classification, and how to exploit a saddle-point hierarchy to accelerate training.

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting of dense Hopfield networks, a student with a single pattern is trained on $M$ examples generated by a teacher with a single planted pattern. The student's ability to infer the teacher pattern defines different phases (paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, spin-glass). The direct problem, where a dense Hopfield network stores $M$ i.i.d. random patterns, has a well-known spin-glass phase where the network freezes into spurious states unrelated to any stored pattern. Prior work established a quiet planting bound: the learning phase of the inverse model extends at least as far as the spin-glass phase of the direct model. However, it was unknown whether the two transitions are exactly identical for $p \geq 3$, because the direct model requires replica symmetry breaking (RSB) corrections while the inverse model on the Nishimori line is replica symmetric. Without this equivalence, the precise location of the spin-glass transition in the direct model remained uncertain due to numerical instability of RSB calculations at large $p$.

In practical machine learning, training data often contains noise, and the generative model (teacher) may have a different architecture than the model used for inference (student). For dense Hopfield networks, the original Hopfield model ($p=2$) has limited noise tolerance: when the teacher's inverse temperature $\beta^*$ is $\mathcal{O}(1)$, the examples are uncorrelated with the teacher pattern, making learning difficult. Prior work on the direct model showed that $p$-body interactions can tolerate extensive noise when storing fewer patterns than the maximum capacity, but the inverse problem (learning from examples) had not been studied for $p \geq 3$. It was unknown whether using a higher-order student could overcome the noise in the teacher's examples, and what scaling of the dataset size would be required.

Adversarial attacks are a major weakness of neural networks, but their theoretical underpinnings are poorly understood. Dense Hopfield networks exhibit variable adversarial robustness depending on the interaction order $p$ and the learning regime, but a quantitative measure of robustness was lacking. In the teacher-student setting with mismatched interaction orders ($p^*=2$, $p \geq 3$), the student can be attacked by replacing some entries of its initial pattern with those of a noisy example, potentially causing it to converge to the example instead of the teacher pattern. Prior work could not predict the critical perturbation size at which this attack succeeds, nor explain why larger datasets improve robustness.

Empirical observations showed that dense Hopfield networks trained by Krotov and Hopfield are adversarially robust in the prototype regime but vulnerable in the feature regime. However, the underlying mechanism was unclear. In the teacher-student setting, the student's learning phases ($eR$, $gR$, $lR$, $SG$, $P$) provide a controlled framework to understand this behavior. Prior theoretical work on adversarial attacks in neural networks did not connect to the phase structure of energy-based models, leaving the relationship between learning regime and robustness unexplained.

The direct $p$-body Hopfield model (with random patterns) has a paramagnetic-to-spin-glass transition that is not captured accurately by the replica-symmetric approximation for $p \geq 3$. Previous 1RSB calculations suffered from numerical instability at large $p$, making the exact transition temperature uncertain. The inverse model (teacher-student) on the Nishimori line is replica symmetric and its $gR$ transition is exact. However, it was not known whether the $gR$ transition of the inverse model coincides with the $P$-$SG$ transition of the direct model for $p \geq 3$, which would provide a way to compute the exact $P$-$SG$ transition.

Restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) are known to have universal approximation properties, but their learning behavior in the teacher-student setting was only understood for small numbers of hidden units. A conjecture stated that the student's performance is independent of the number of hidden units when teacher patterns are uncorrelated, based on empirical observations and analytical results for $P=P^*=1$ and $P=P^*=2$. However, it was not known whether this independence holds for arbitrary finite $P$ and $P^*$, or whether the factorization property (an RBM with $P$ uncorrelated hidden units factorizes into $P$ RBMs with one hidden unit each) extends beyond $P=2$.

Overparameterized neural networks often learn low-dimensional representations, but the mechanism is not well understood. In RBMs, it was observed that when the student has more hidden units than necessary, some units may not learn meaningful features. Prior work on the teacher-student setting with $P=P^*=2$ found a PSB solution where student patterns learn teacher patterns one-to-one, but it was unknown whether this extends to $P > P^*$ and whether the extra hidden units remain in a spin-glass phase. Understanding this low-dimensional learning strategy could provide insights into the lottery ticket hypothesis and network pruning.

The lottery ticket hypothesis states that overparameterized neural networks contain subnetworks (winning tickets) that, when trained in isolation, achieve comparable accuracy to the full network and converge faster. However, the theoretical understanding of why certain initial conditions are fortuitous is limited. Existing studies rely on large-scale empirical pruning in deep networks. A simple, analytically tractable model that exhibits the lottery ticket phenomenon would help identify the key ingredients. The RBM teacher-student setting with uncorrelated patterns provides such a model, but it was not known whether magnitude pruning could identify winning tickets in this setting.

Real-world data often exhibits correlations between features, which can aid learning. In the teacher-student setting for RBMs, the effect of correlations between teacher patterns on the critical data load was only understood for $P=P^*=2$. For larger numbers of hidden units, the dependence of $\alpha_{\text{crit}}$ on $P^*$ and correlation strength $c$ was unknown. Understanding this dependence is important because it reveals how the structure of data (correlations between abstract concepts) influences the amount of data needed for learning, and could inform regularization strategies like decorrelation.

In unsupervised learning, neural networks often undergo a sequence of phase transitions during training, starting with a low-rank approximation and progressively learning more detailed structure. For RBMs with $P=P^*=2$ and correlated teacher patterns, three ferromagnetic phases (SSB, $\text{PSB}_s$, $\text{PSB}_t$) were identified. However, it was unknown whether this phenomenology extends to larger numbers of hidden units, and how the critical loads for the transitions depend on $P$ and the correlation strength $c$. Understanding these transitions is crucial for explaining the multistage learning dynamics observed in RBMs trained on real data.

Dense associative memory (DAM) models are energy-based models that learn interpretable prototypes, but their loss landscape and stationary points are not well characterized. Prior work studied the teacher-student setting for RBMs and Hopfield networks, but not for DAMs with von Mises-Fisher distributions and categorical priors. Understanding the stationary points of DAMs is important for explaining their learning dynamics and for developing efficient training algorithms. The relationship between maximum likelihood estimation and posterior sampling in the teacher-student setting was not established for this class of models.

Training DAMs with a fixed inverse temperature $\beta$ becomes unstable as the number of hidden units $P$ increases: many memories get stuck in noisy states that do not contribute to classification. Lowering $\beta$ helps convergence but reduces resolution and diversity, lowering accuracy. Annealing schedules can help but are difficult to tune. The teacher-student analysis revealed that the effective inverse temperature should be $\beta_{\text{eff}} = \varsigma\beta$ with $\varsigma < 1$ when the teacher has finite noise, suggesting that a regularized loss with a reduced effective temperature could improve training. However, this regularization had not been tested empirically.

The loss landscape of neural networks is known to contain many saddle points, but their structure is poorly understood. For DAMs, it was observed that learning dynamics follow a tree of permutation symmetry-breaking bifurcations, suggesting that saddles corresponding to symmetric states play a key role. However, it was not known whether the stationary points of narrower DAMs are embedded as saddles in wider DAMs, which would explain the tree structure and provide a theoretical basis for network-growing algorithms. Prior work on the embedding principle for feedforward networks did not cover energy-based models like DAMs.

Training large DAMs is computationally expensive, with training time scaling linearly with the number of hidden units. The saddle-point hierarchy principle suggests that wider DAMs contain the solutions of narrower DAMs as saddles, implying that one could start with a small network and grow it during training. However, it was not known whether a practical algorithm could exploit this hierarchy to accelerate training without sacrificing accuracy. Prior network-growing methods like splitting steepest descent had been applied to feedforward networks but not to energy-based models like DAMs.

Interpretability is a desirable property for neural networks, but most deep learning models are black boxes. Dense associative memories have been shown to learn interpretable prototypes in supervised settings, but it was unknown whether this interpretability extends to unsupervised learning. The DAM model derived from a Boltzmann machine with categorical priors offers a natural framework for interpretable classification, but its ability to discover meaningful latent classes without labels had not been demonstrated.

In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks, the inverse model (student) learns a teacher pattern from examples generated by a teacher network. The direct model is a dense Hopfield network with \(M\) random memorized patterns. On the Nishimori line, where the student has the same interaction order \(p\) and inverse temperature \(\beta\) as the teacher (\(p=p^*\), \(\beta=\beta^*\)), the global retrieval phase (\(gR\)) of the inverse model—where the student can retrieve the teacher pattern from any initial condition—coincides with the spin-glass phase of the direct model—where the network freezes in random states with zero magnetization \(m\) (overlap with any stored memory) and positive spin-glass order parameter \(q\) (overlap between two replicas). This refines the quiet planting bound, which states that the learning phase of the inverse model extends at least as far as the spin-glass phase of the direct model, by showing that the learning phase extends exactly as far.

metadata.narrative: The equivalence between the gR transition of the inverse model and the P-SG transition of the direct model is supported by a theoretical argument based on quiet planting and contiguity, but this argument assumes replica symmetry on the Nishimori line (P1). The Monte Carlo simulations for p=3 (H1) provide strong numerical evidence that the RS solution is accurate for this case, mitigating the risk. The dominant risk is that replica symmetry breaking could occur for larger p or different parameters, which would invalidate the equivalence. The highlight H1 directly addresses this risk for p=3, but the conclusion's generality to all p relies on the unproven assumption. The layer of unreliability is the theoretical foundation for p>3; the quantitative phase diagram for p=3 is well-supported by simulations.

nodes.title: Equivalence of the global retrieval phase of the inverse model on the Nishimori line and the spin-glass phase of the direct model

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks with mismatched interaction orders, a student network with interaction order \(p \geq 3\) can learn a teacher pattern from a teacher with interaction order \(p^*=2\) even when the teacher's inverse temperature \(\beta^*\) scales as \(\mathcal{O}(N^{2/p-1})\) (i.e., the teacher noise is extensive), provided the student is given \(M \sim \mathcal{O}(N^{p-1})\) examples, where \(N\) is the number of components per pattern. For \(p=4\), this yields a noise tolerance of \(\mathcal{O}(N^{1/2})\), meaning the teacher's inverse temperature can be as low as \(\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})\). The student's learning performance is optimal when the effective inverse temperature \(\lambda = \frac{[\beta^*]^{p/2}}{(p/2)!} N^{p/2-1}\) equals the student's inverse temperature \(\beta\).

metadata.narrative: The extensive noise tolerance claim is derived using a cumulant expansion that may have neglected higher-order terms (P2). However, Monte Carlo simulations for p=4 (H2) confirm the predicted behavior, showing that the student can retrieve the teacher pattern even with O(N^{-1/2}) noise. The simulations validate the qualitative and quantitative predictions for the tested case. The main risk is that the cumulant expansion might break down for other values of p or N, but the simulations provide a sanity check. The conclusion is well-supported for p=4, and the theoretical derivation provides a plausible mechanism for general p.

nodes.title: Extensive noise tolerance with mismatched interaction orders in the large-noise scaling

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks with teacher interaction order \(p^*=2\), student interaction order \(p \geq 3\) (even), and zero student temperature (\(\beta = \infty\)), the student pattern is initialized as a mixture of the teacher pattern and a single noisy example \(\sigma^a\): a fraction \(\varepsilon\) of its entries are taken from \(\sigma^a\) and the rest from the teacher pattern. The largest fraction \(\varepsilon^*\) for which the student still converges to the teacher pattern (rather than to the example) is \(\varepsilon^* = \frac{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}}{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}+1}\), where \(\alpha = \frac{M(p/2+1)!}{N^{p/2}}\) is the finite-noise load (with \(M\) the number of examples and \(N\) the pattern dimension), and \(\eta\) is a parameter depending on the teacher's inverse temperature \(\beta^*\) and \(p\) (for \(p=4\), \(\eta = \frac{2[\beta^*]^2}{(1-2\beta^*)^2}\)). This formula shows that adversarial robustness increases monotonically with the dataset size \(\alpha\).

metadata.narrative: The adversarial robustness formula is derived under the assumption that the attacking example has zero overlap with the teacher pattern (P3). Monte Carlo simulations for p=4 (H3) show that the formula accurately predicts the critical perturbation size even when the example with largest overlap is used, indicating that the assumption is not restrictive in practice. The formula is also validated for typical examples. The risk that the formula might fail for other attack strategies is mitigated by the simulation results. The conclusion is strongly supported by both theory and experiment.

nodes.title: Exact formula for adversarial robustness at zero temperature for mismatched interaction orders

nodes.content: In dense Hopfield networks, adversarial robustness depends on the learning regime. The example Retrieval phase (\(eR\)), also called the prototype phase, is inherently robust because retrieving an example is equivalent to recovering the teacher pattern (the signal). In contrast, the global Retrieval phase (\(gR\)), also called the feature phase, can be vulnerable when it overlaps with the inaccurate \(eR\) phase, where the student pattern has finite overlap with a noisy example but zero overlap with the teacher pattern. Increasing the dataset size \(\alpha\) (the number of examples per pattern dimension) stabilizes the \(gR\) phase and increases robustness, which explains why larger neural networks are often more adversarially robust.

metadata.narrative: The clarification of adversarial robustness dependence on learning regime is a qualitative explanation based on the phase diagram. No specific weak points were identified beyond the general limitations of the teacher-student setting. The phase diagrams (Fig. 2.6) clearly show the overlap between gR and inaccurate eR phases, providing a direct mechanistic explanation. The conclusion is well-supported by the theoretical framework.

nodes.title: Clarification of adversarial robustness dependence on learning regime in dense Hopfield networks

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks on the Nishimori line (where the student has the same interaction order \(p\) and inverse temperature \(\beta\) as the teacher: \(p=p^*\), \(\beta=\beta^*\)), the global retrieval (\(gR\)) phase transition of the inverse model coincides with the exact paramagnetic-to-spin-glass (\(P\)-\(SG\)) phase transition of the direct model (a dense Hopfield network with \(M\) random patterns) for any \(p\), provided the temperature \(T = 1/\beta\) is above the critical temperature \(T_{\text{crit}}\) of the direct model with a single pattern. This equivalence allows the \(P\)-\(SG\) transition to be located precisely using the replica-symmetric (RS) solution of the inverse model, which avoids the numerical instability that arises in one-step replica symmetry breaking (1RSB) calculations for the direct model at large \(p\).

metadata.narrative: This conclusion is essentially the same as Conclusion 1 but from the perspective of the direct model. The same weak point (P1) and highlight (H1) apply. The precise location of the P-SG transition is obtained from the inverse model's gR transition, which is validated for p=3 by simulations. The risk is that the equivalence might not hold for larger p, but the theoretical argument and the p=3 validation provide reasonable support.

nodes.title: Precise location of the paramagnetic-to-spin-glass transition in the direct model via the inverse model on the Nishimori line

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting for restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) with binary visible and hidden units, where the teacher has \(P^*\) hidden units with uncorrelated patterns (covariance matrix \(\mathcal{Q} = \mathbf{I}\)) and the student has \(P\) hidden units, the student's learning performance, measured by the magnetization \(m\) (the expected overlap between a teacher pattern and a student pattern), is independent of \(P\) and \(P^*\) for any finite \(P, P^*\). The critical data load \(\alpha_{\text{crit}} = M/N\) (where \(M\) is the number of training examples and \(N\) the number of visible units) above which learning becomes possible is \(\alpha_{\text{crit}} = 1/[\beta^*\beta]^2\), which also does not depend on \(P\) or \(P^*\). This validates the conjecture of Barra et al. (2017) and generalizes the results of Hou et al. (2019) from \(P=P^*=2\) to arbitrary finite \(P\) and \(P^*\).

metadata.narrative: The independence of learning performance from the number of hidden units is derived under the PSB ansatz (P4). The analytical factorization (H4) provides a rigorous derivation within RS, and simulations confirm the PSB solution is realized for P=2. However, the existence of partial PSB solutions means the independence is not guaranteed for all initial conditions. The dominant risk is that the student may converge to a partial PSB state, especially for larger P. The highlight H4 shows that the PSB solution is at least a valid fixed point, but the conclusion's generality depends on the stability of this solution.

nodes.title: Independence of learning performance from number of hidden units for uncorrelated teacher patterns in RBMs

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting for restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) with uncorrelated teacher patterns (covariance \(\mathcal{Q} = \mathbf{I}\)), under the permutation symmetry breaking (PSB) ansatz, an RBM with \(P\) hidden units factorizes into \(P\) independent RBMs with one hidden unit each. When the student has more hidden units than the teacher (\(P > P^*\)), exactly \(P^*\) student patterns learn the teacher patterns one-to-one, with magnetization \(m\) (overlap with teacher pattern) and spin-glass overlap \(q\) (overlap between two independent student replicas) satisfying \(m = q\). The remaining \(P - P^*\) student patterns freeze in spin-glass states with zero magnetization and a different spin-glass overlap \(g\). This demonstrates an implicitly low-dimensional learning strategy, where only a subset of hidden units are used to learn the data.

metadata.narrative: The factorization and low-dimensional learning in overparameterized RBMs is a direct consequence of the PSB ansatz. The same weak point (P4) applies: the PSB solution may not be the only attractor. The analytical derivation (H4) shows that the extra hidden units can freeze in spin-glass states, providing a mechanism for low-dimensional learning. The risk is that in practice, the extra units may also learn features (partial PSB). The conclusion is well-supported as a possible learning strategy, but not as the only one.

nodes.title: Factorization and low-dimensional learning in overparameterized RBMs under the PSB ansatz

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting for restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) with uncorrelated teacher patterns (covariance \(\mathcal{Q} = \mathbf{I}\)) and an overparameterized student (\(P > P^*\)), a variant of magnitude pruning can identify a winning ticket. After training a student with \(P=8\) real-valued patterns (initialized as i.i.d. Gaussian) on data generated by a teacher with \(P^*=4\) patterns, the \(P^*=4\) student patterns with the largest Euclidean norm are selected. When retrained from their initial conditions, this subnetwork converges faster than a randomly initialized network of the same size (\(P=4\)). The lead of the winning ticket diminishes over time due to the ergodicity of the training algorithm (underdamped Langevin dynamics). This provides a toy model for the lottery ticket hypothesis.

metadata.narrative: The toy model of the lottery ticket hypothesis is an empirical demonstration. No specific weak points were identified beyond the limited scope (single experiment, specific pruning method). The experiment shows that magnitude pruning can identify a winning ticket that converges faster initially. The conclusion is modest ("can serve as a toy model") and is supported by the data. The main limitation is the lack of comparison with other pruning methods and the synthetic data setting.

nodes.title: Toy model of the lottery ticket hypothesis in the teacher-student RBM setting

First, a spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) phase occurs, where all student patterns converge to a single configuration with equal overlap with all teacher patterns. Next, a student permutation symmetry breaking (\(	ext{PSB}_s\)) phase occurs, where student patterns differentiate into distinct configurations with equal overlaps with the teacher patterns. Finally, a teacher permutation symmetry breaking (\(	ext{PSB}_t\)) phase occurs, where student patterns learn teacher patterns one-to-one. The critical loads for \(	ext{PSB}_s\) and \(	ext{PSB}_t\) depend on the number of hidden units \(P\) and the correlation strength \(c\).

The qualitative picture (SSB, PSB_s, PSB_t) is likely correct, but the quantitative critical loads are uncertain. The highlight is that the phenomenology extends to P=3, but the RS approximation's failure at large c means the precise phase boundaries are not reliable. The conclusion is partially supported; the qualitative sequence is plausible, but the quantitative predictions should be treated with caution.

nodes.content: In a dense associative memory (DAM) model with a von Mises-Fisher distribution on the data layer and categorical (one-hot) priors on the hidden and class layers, the stationary points of the negative log-likelihood loss satisfy a set of self-consistent equations for the weight vectors \(\mathbf{w}^\mu\) (normalized to unit norm) and the class probability matrix \(\mathbf{p}\) (constrained to have fixed row and column sums). In the teacher-student setting, where a student DAM learns from data generated by a teacher DAM, the fixed points of the posterior sampling satisfy analogous saddle-point equations. In the limit of large data (\(\varrho = M/(P^*N) \to \infty\), where \(M\) is the number of examples, \(P^*\) the number of teacher hidden units, and \(N\) the data dimension) and low teacher noise (\(v = \beta^*/N \to \infty\), where \(\beta^*\) is the teacher inverse temperature), the teacher-student equations reduce to the maximum likelihood stationary conditions, establishing an equivalence between the two frameworks.

metadata.narrative: The saddle-point equations for DAM stationary points and the teacher-student equivalence are derived analytically. No weak points were identified beyond the general limitations of the replica method. The derivation is rigorous within the stated assumptions (RS, large N limit). The equivalence in the limit of large data and low teacher noise is mathematically established. The conclusion is well-supported by the theoretical derivation.

nodes.title: Equivalence between DAM stationary points and teacher-student fixed points in the large-data, low-noise limit

nodes.content: Training a dense associative memory (DAM) model by minimizing the effective loss \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{p}) = -\frac{1}{P^*} \sum_{\mu=1}^{P^*} \sum_{y=0}^C q_y^{*\mu} \log \mathcal{P}_{\beta,\varsigma}(\mathbf{x}^{*\mu}, y|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{p})\), where \(\mathcal{P}_{\beta,\varsigma}(\mathbf{x}, y|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{\mu=1}^P p_y^\mu \frac{\exp(\varsigma\beta \sum_i w_i^\mu x_i)}{\Omega_N(\beta)} + p_y^0 \frac{1}{\Omega_N(0)}\) with a regularization parameter \(\varsigma < 1\) (so that the effective inverse temperature is \(\varsigma\beta\)), significantly improves training stability and classification accuracy compared to standard maximum likelihood training (which corresponds to \(\varsigma=1\)). On the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits, this method achieves 96% classification accuracy with \(P=1000\) hidden units, compared to 91% with standard training at \(\beta=18\) and 79% at \(\beta=6\). The parameter \(\varsigma\) mimics the noise present in the data generation process.

metadata.narrative: The effective loss regularization improves training stability, as demonstrated on MNIST (H6). The weak point is that the regularization parameter ς is chosen heuristically (P7). The improvement is significant and visually clear, but the method's generalizability is untested. The highlight H6 shows a concrete improvement on a standard benchmark, but the lack of a principled way to choose ς limits the conclusion's impact. The conclusion is supported for the specific case tested, but further validation is needed.

nodes.title: Effective loss regularization improves training stability and accuracy in DAMs

nodes.content: In a dense associative memory (DAM) model, if a set of parameters (the weight vectors \(\mathbf{w}^\mu\), the class probability matrix \(\mathbf{p}\), and the overlaps \(m^{\mu_*\mu}\)) is a fixed point of the saddle-point equations (which characterize stationary points of the loss) for a DAM with \(P\) hidden units, then a duplicated set of parameters, where \(R \leq P\) of the hidden units are copied (their weight vectors are duplicated, their class probabilities are halved, and the hidden unit prior is adjusted accordingly), forms a fixed point for a DAM with \(P+R\) hidden units. For sufficiently large inverse temperature \(\beta\), this duplicated fixed point is a saddle point (not a local minimum). This establishes that wider DAMs contain the stationary points of narrower DAMs as saddle points.

metadata.narrative: The saddle-point hierarchy principle is proven analytically (H7). The weak point is that the proof assumes large β (P8). The proof is rigorous for sufficiently large β, but the threshold is not specified. The highlight H7 provides a strong theoretical foundation. The risk is that for the β values used in practice, the duplicated fixed points might not be saddles. However, the empirical success of the splitting algorithm (H8) suggests that the saddle property holds in practice. The conclusion is well-supported by theory and experiment.

nodes.title: Saddle-point hierarchy principle for DAMs: wider networks contain narrower stationary points as saddles

nodes.content: The splitting steepest descent algorithm (Algorithm 1) exploits the saddle-point hierarchy of dense associative memories (DAMs) by starting training with a small number of hidden units and progressively duplicating them. This reduces training time from linear in the maximum number of hidden units \(P_{\text{max}}\) to approximately logarithmic in \(P_{\text{max}}\). On the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets, DAMs trained with splitting achieve comparable classification accuracy to those trained without splitting (with \(P_{\text{max}}\) hidden units from the start), but with significantly reduced computational cost, especially for large \(P_{\text{max}}\).

metadata.narrative: The splitting steepest descent algorithm accelerates training, as demonstrated on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST (H8). The weak point is that the computational overhead of eigenvector computation is not fully accounted for (P9). The empirical speedup is substantial and consistent, suggesting that the overhead is not prohibitive. The highlight H8 shows a clear practical benefit. The conclusion is well-supported for the tested datasets and architectures.

nodes.title: Accelerated DAM training via splitting steepest descent exploiting the saddle-point hierarchy

nodes.content: The dense associative memory (DAM) model learns interpretable prototypes (memories) in both supervised and unsupervised classification settings. In supervised training on MNIST, each memory \(\mathbf{w}^\mu\) (a weight vector normalized to unit norm) is associated with a soft label \(\mathbf{p}^\mu/p_{\mathbf{h}}(\mu)\) (the class probability vector for that memory, normalized by the hidden unit prior) that corresponds to a digit class. Approximately 98% of test data points are classified into the class of the memory they most resemble (1-nearest neighbor fidelity). In unsupervised training using a minimum entropy regularization (Eq. 4.15: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{unsup}}(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{p}) = -\frac{1}{P^*} \sum_{\mu=1}^{P^*} \sum_{y=0}^{C} [(1-\varepsilon)\mathcal{P}_{\beta,\varsigma}(y|\mathbf{x}^{*\mu};\mathbf{w},\mathbf{p}) + \varepsilon\frac{1}{C+1}] \log \mathcal{P}_{\beta,\varsigma}(\mathbf{x}^{*\mu},y|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{p})\)), the DAM discovers latent classes that correspond to digit types, as shown by the learned class weights.

metadata.narrative: The DAM learns interpretable prototypes in supervised and unsupervised settings, as shown by visual inspection and the 1-NN fidelity metric (H9). The weak point is that interpretability is not quantitatively defined (P10). The visual evidence and the fidelity metric provide some support, but the claim of interpretability is subjective. The highlight H9 shows that the model discovers meaningful structure, but the conclusion's strength is limited by the lack of a rigorous interpretability measure.

nodes.title: Interpretable prototypes learned by DAMs in supervised and unsupervised classification

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks on the Nishimori line (where the student has the same interaction order \(p\) and inverse temperature \(\beta\) as the teacher: \(p=p^*\), \(\beta=\beta^*\)), the claim that the global retrieval (\(gR\)) phase transition of the student coincides with the paramagnetic-to-spin-glass (\(P\)-\(SG\)) transition of the direct model (a dense Hopfield network with \(M\) random patterns) relies on the assumption that the student's posterior distribution is replica symmetric. The paper does not provide a rigorous proof that replica symmetry holds for all \(p \geq 3\) on the Nishimori line; it only cites Nishimori identities and states that the system is 'expected' to be replica symmetric. If replica symmetry breaking occurs, the \(gR\) transition could differ from the \(P\)-\(SG\) transition.

metadata.failure_mode: If replica symmetry breaking occurs on the Nishimori line, the free entropy of the inverse model would differ from the RS expression, and the gR transition (defined by the RS solution) would not correspond to the true phase transition. Consequently, the claimed equivalence with the direct model's P-SG transition would fail, and the precise location of the P-SG transition derived from the inverse model would be incorrect. The conclusion that the learning phase extends exactly as far as the spin-glass phase would be invalidated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper asserts that the inverse model on the Nishimori line is replica symmetric based on Nishimori identities, but this is a standard belief rather than a proven theorem for p≥3. The replica method is non-rigorous, and the RS solution may not be exact even on the Nishimori line for all parameter regimes. The paper does not check the stability of the RS solution against RSB perturbations, nor does it provide a rigorous argument that the Nishimori identities guarantee replica symmetry for this specific model. Without this guarantee, the equivalence between the gR transition and the P-SG transition is not firmly established.

nodes.title: Replica symmetry on the Nishimori line is assumed, not proven

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks with teacher interaction order \(p^*=2\) and student order \(p=4\), the derivation of the large-noise scaling regime (where the teacher's inverse temperature \(\beta^* \sim \mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})\) and the number of examples \(M \sim \mathcal{O}(N^3)\)) uses a cumulant expansion of the teacher-student coupling truncated at order \(p/2+1 = 3\). The paper does not verify that the neglected higher-order terms are subdominant for the system sizes used in simulations (\(N=256\)). If these terms contribute at leading order, the predicted noise tolerance and the effective parameter \(\lambda = \frac{[\beta^*]^{p/2}}{(p/2)!} N^{p/2-1}\) might be incorrect.

metadata.failure_mode: If the neglected higher-order terms contribute at leading order, the effective coupling between teacher and student would be different from the form assumed (β λ α ...). The resulting saddle-point equations would change, and the predicted noise tolerance (β* ~ O(N^{2/p-1})) might not hold. The quantitative phase diagram in Fig. 2.6 could be inaccurate, and the conclusion that a p=4 student can tolerate O(N^{1/2}) noise would be unsupported.
metadata.weakness_reason: The cumulant expansion is truncated at the first non-vanishing order that couples teacher and student terms. The paper argues that higher-order terms are subdominant in N, but does not provide a rigorous bound or check for the specific scaling used. For finite N, the neglected terms could be of comparable magnitude, especially if β* is not exactly O(N^{2/p-1}) but has a different prefactor. The paper does not test the sensitivity of the results to the truncation order.

nodes.title: Cumulant expansion truncation for mismatched interaction orders may neglect leading-order terms

nodes.content: In the derivation of the adversarial robustness formula \(\varepsilon^* = \frac{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}}{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}+1}\) for a student dense Hopfield network with teacher interaction order \(p^*=2\), student order \(p \geq 3\), and zero student temperature (\(\beta = \infty\)), it is assumed that the example \(\sigma^a\) used for the attack has zero overlap with the teacher pattern: \(m^* = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \xi_i^* \sigma_i^a = 0\). For finite \(N\), the overlap is \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N})\) and can be non-zero for specific examples. The paper does not provide a rigorous bound on how deviations from \(m^* = 0\) affect \(\varepsilon^*\); it only shows numerically that the formula still approximates the robustness when the example with the largest overlap is used. If the attack uses an example with a significantly non-zero overlap, the formula may overestimate the true robustness.

metadata.failure_mode: If the attacking example has a non-zero overlap with the teacher pattern, the expressions for r* and k in the derivation would change, leading to a different condition for retrieval. The formula ε* would no longer be exact, and the predicted robustness could be either too high or too low. The conclusion that ε* is given by that closed form would be invalid for attacks using examples with non-zero overlap, which are likely in practice.
metadata.weakness_reason: The derivation uses the law of large numbers to set the overlap between the teacher pattern and the attacking example to zero. However, for any finite N, the overlap is a random variable with variance 1/N. The paper does not analyze how the formula changes when this overlap is non-zero, nor does it provide a probabilistic bound on the error. The numerical test with the example having the largest overlap shows that the formula still works reasonably well, but this is only one test case and does not constitute a general proof.

nodes.title: Adversarial robustness formula assumes zero overlap with attacking example

nodes.content: In the teacher-student setting for restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) with uncorrelated teacher patterns (covariance \(\mathcal{Q} = \mathbf{I}\)), the claim that the student's learning performance (magnetization \(m\)) is independent of the number of hidden units \(P\) and \(P^*\) relies on the Permutation Symmetry Breaking (PSB) ansatz being the globally stable solution of the saddle-point equations. The paper shows that the PSB solution has higher free entropy than partial PSB solutions (where multiple student patterns converge to the same teacher pattern) within the replica-symmetric (RS) approximation, but this comparison may not hold under replica symmetry breaking. Moreover, Monte Carlo simulations with random initial conditions show that the student can converge to partial PSB solutions, indicating that the PSB solution is not always reached. Therefore, the independence result may not hold for all training trajectories.

metadata.failure_mode: If the student converges to a partial PSB solution instead of the PSB solution, the magnetization m would be different from the single-unit solution, and the performance would depend on P and P*. The conclusion that the student's performance is independent of the number of hidden units would be false for those training trajectories. The claim that the critical load α_crit does not depend on P or P* might still hold, but the quantitative value of m would be affected.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper assumes the PSB ansatz to derive the factorization, but does not prove that this ansatz is the only stable solution of the full saddle-point equations. The existence of partial PSB solutions with different magnetizations shows that the system has multiple fixed points. The RS free entropy comparison favors PSB, but RSB could alter the free energy landscape. The simulations show that the system can get stuck in partial PSB states, so the independence result is not guaranteed for all initial conditions or training algorithms.

nodes.title: Independence of performance from hidden units relies on PSB ansatz stability

nodes.title: Symmetry-breaking phase transitions rely on RS approximation

nodes.content: In the dense associative memory (DAM) model trained on the MNIST dataset, the effective loss regularization parameter \(\varsigma\) (which controls the effective inverse temperature \(\varsigma\beta\) in the loss) is set to 0.25 by hand. The paper does not provide a principled method to determine the optimal \(\varsigma\) for a given dataset, nor does it compare against other regularization techniques (e.g., weight decay, dropout, annealing). The improvement in accuracy (from 91% to 96%) is demonstrated only on MNIST with \(P=1000\) hidden units; the generalizability to other datasets and architectures is unknown.

metadata.failure_mode: If the optimal ς varies significantly across datasets, the effective loss regularization may not generalize. The conclusion that training with the effective loss improves stability and accuracy would be limited to the specific setting tested. Without a principled way to choose ς, the method cannot be reliably applied to new problems, and the claimed improvement may not hold.
metadata.weakness_reason: The choice of ς=0.25 is not derived from theory or a systematic search; it is selected based on empirical performance on MNIST. The paper does not explore the sensitivity of the results to ς, nor does it provide guidelines for selecting ς for other datasets. The comparison is against standard training with fixed β, not against other common regularization methods, so it is unclear whether the improvement is due to the specific form of the effective loss or simply due to having an additional hyperparameter.

nodes.title: Effective loss regularization parameter is chosen heuristically

nodes.content: In the dense associative memory (DAM) model, the proof that the duplicated fixed point (where some hidden units are copied) is a saddle point (not a local minimum) relies on the assumption that the effective inverse temperature \(\beta_{\text{eff}} = \varsigma\beta\) is sufficiently large so that the softmax function approximates a step function. The paper does not derive a precise condition on \(\beta_{\text{eff}}\) for the saddle property to hold, nor does it verify numerically for the values of \(\beta\) used in training (e.g., \(\beta=18\)). If \(\beta\) is not large enough, the duplicated fixed point might be a local minimum, and the splitting steepest descent algorithm might not escape it.

metadata.failure_mode: If β is not large enough, the duplicated fixed point could be a local minimum rather than a saddle. In that case, the splitting steepest descent algorithm would not be able to escape it by descending along the eigenvector, and the network would not learn new features after splitting. The conclusion that wider DAMs contain the stationary points of narrower DAMs as saddle points would be false for the parameter regime used in practice, undermining the theoretical basis for the acceleration algorithm.
metadata.weakness_reason: The proof in Appendix 4.I shows that the quadratic form for a certain direction is positive when β_eff is large, but does not provide a threshold. The argument uses the approximation that the softmax becomes a step function, which is valid only in the limit β_eff → ∞. For finite β_eff, the softmax is smooth, and the quadratic form could be negative, making the duplicated fixed point a local minimum. The paper does not check this condition for the β values used in experiments.

nodes.title: Saddle-point hierarchy proof assumes large β

nodes.content: In the comparison of training time between splitting steepest descent and standard training for dense associative memories (DAMs) on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, the reported training time includes the time for computing eigenvectors of the splitting matrices (used to identify which hidden units to duplicate and to escape saddle points). However, the paper does not provide a detailed breakdown of the computational cost, nor does it compare the total number of floating-point operations. The eigenvector computation adds overhead per epoch, which may offset the gains from using fewer hidden units initially. The observed speedup may be implementation-dependent.

metadata.failure_mode: If the eigenvector computation overhead is significant, the actual speedup of splitting steepest descent over standard training could be much smaller than reported, or even negative for small P_max. The conclusion that training time is reduced from linear to logarithmic in P_max would be misleading if the constant factors are large. The practical benefit of the algorithm would be diminished.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper reports wall-clock time, which can be affected by implementation details, hardware, and background processes. The eigenvector computation using the Rayleigh quotient minimization (Appendix 4.K) requires additional forward and backward passes through the network. The paper does not quantify this overhead or compare the total number of epochs or gradient evaluations between the two methods. Without such analysis, it is unclear whether the speedup is due to the algorithm itself or to implementation optimizations.

nodes.title: Splitting steepest descent training time comparison may not account for eigenvector computation overhead

nodes.content: In the dense associative memory (DAM) model, the claim that the learned memories are interpretable prototypes is based on visual inspection of the weight vectors. The paper does not provide a quantitative metric for interpretability (e.g., faithfulness of the 1-nearest neighbor classifier based on the memories, or comparison with other interpretable models). The unsupervised classification experiment uses a heuristic minimum entropy regularization with a handpicked parameter \(\varepsilon\), and the resulting class assignments are not validated against ground truth labels. The interpretability may not extend to more complex datasets.

metadata.failure_mode: If the interpretability claim is based solely on visual inspection, it is not scientifically rigorous. The conclusion that the DAM learns interpretable prototypes would be unsupported by quantitative evidence. The unsupervised classification result may not replicate on other datasets, and the method for unsupervised training may require significant tuning. The claim that the DAM is interpretable in both supervised and unsupervised settings would be overstated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper states that approximately 98% of test data points are classified into the class of the memory they most resemble, but this is a property of the trained model, not a measure of interpretability. Interpretability is a subjective concept; the paper does not define it operationally. The unsupervised experiment on MNIST patches shows that the memories resemble digits, but this is a simple dataset; the method may not discover meaningful latent classes on more complex data. The choice of ε in Eq. 4.15 is not justified.

nodes.title: Interpretability claim is qualitative and not quantitatively validated

nodes.content: For the dense Hopfield network with p=3 on the Nishimori line (β=β*), Monte Carlo simulations with N=512 units and L=100 student replicas (Fig. 2.4) show that the student-teacher overlap q* and the spin-glass overlap q obtained from the simulations agree with the numerical solution of the replica-symmetric saddle-point equations (Eqs. 2.5) across a range of data loads α, with deviations attributable to finite-size effects (Fig. 2.9). This agreement provides numerical evidence that the RS solution is accurate for p=3, supporting the equivalence claim for this case.

metadata.credit: The Monte Carlo simulations directly test the RS prediction for the order parameters on the Nishimori line. The agreement within finite-size error bars shows that the RS solution is not just a theoretical construct but accurately describes the behavior of the finite system for p=3. This preempts the failure mode that the RS solution might be incorrect due to replica symmetry breaking, at least for p=3. The simulations underwrite the quantitative phase diagram (Fig. 2.2) and thus the equivalence between the gR transition and the P-SG transition for p=3. Without these simulations, the conclusion would rely solely on the unproven assumption of replica symmetry.

nodes.title: Monte Carlo simulations validate RS solution for p=3 on Nishimori line

nodes.content: For the teacher-student setting with p*=2, p=4, and large-noise scaling (β* ~ O(N^{-1/2}), M ~ O(N^3)), Monte Carlo simulations with N=256 units and L=100 student replicas (Fig. 2.7) show that the student-teacher overlap q* as a function of α and β agrees with the RS saddle-point solution. The simulations confirm that a student with p=4 can retrieve the teacher pattern even when the teacher's inverse temperature is as low as O(N^{-1/2}), validating the extensive noise tolerance prediction.

metadata.credit: The simulations directly demonstrate that the student can learn from extremely noisy data, which is the central claim of the conclusion. They validate the cumulant expansion and the RS solution for the specific case of p=4, N=256. Without these simulations, the theoretical derivation would be untested, and the conclusion would be speculative. The simulations underwrite the quantitative phase diagram (Fig. 2.6) and show that the predicted noise tolerance is realizable in a finite system.

nodes.title: Monte Carlo simulations confirm extensive noise tolerance for p=4

nodes.content: For the teacher-student setting with p*=2, p=4, zero temperature, and finite-noise scaling (η=1), Monte Carlo simulations with N=1024 units and L=100 student replicas (Fig. 2.8) show that the analytical formula ε* = α^{1/3}/(α^{1/3}+1) accurately predicts the critical perturbation size at which the student's overlap with the teacher pattern drops to zero, for both typical examples and the example with largest overlap. The agreement is quantitative across a range of α.

metadata.credit: The simulations provide strong empirical support that the derived formula is exact under the stated assumptions. They test the formula against two different attack strategies (typical example and worst-case example) and show it works in both cases. This preempts the failure mode that the formula might only hold for the idealized typical example. The simulations underwrite the conclusion that adversarial robustness increases monotonically with dataset size α, as predicted by the formula.

nodes.title: Monte Carlo simulations validate adversarial robustness formula for p=4

nodes.content: For RBMs with uncorrelated teacher patterns (Q=I), the paper analytically shows that under the Permutation Symmetry Breaking (PSB) ansatz, the saddle-point equations (Eqs. 3.14) factorize into P independent systems of equations, each identical to the single-hidden-unit case (Eqs. 3.20, 3.22). This factorization is derived within the RS approximation and is validated by Monte Carlo simulations for P=2, P*=1 (Fig. 3.5) and P=2, P*=2 (Fig. 3.4), where the student's magnetization matches the single-unit solution.

metadata.credit: The analytical factorization provides a rigorous derivation (within RS) of the independence of performance from the number of hidden units. The simulations confirm that the PSB solution is realized in practice for the tested cases. This preempts the failure mode that the factorization might be an artifact of the RS approximation. The factorization underlies the conclusions about low-dimensional learning and the lottery ticket hypothesis, making it a load-bearing theoretical result.

nodes.title: Analytical factorization of saddle-point equations for uncorrelated patterns

nodes.content: For RBMs with uniformly correlated teacher patterns, the paper derives a closed-form expression for the critical load α_crit = 1/([β*β]^2 λ_max^S) with λ_max^S = (P*-1)^2 c d + (P*-1)(c+d) + 1 (Eq. 3.24). This generalizes the P*=2 result of Hou et al. (2019) to arbitrary finite P*. The formula is validated by numerical solutions of the RS saddle-point equations (Fig. 3.10) and by Monte Carlo simulations for P=P*=2,3 (Fig. 3.14) on the Nishimori line.

metadata.credit: The closed-form expression provides a clear, interpretable prediction for how data correlations and the number of hidden units affect the amount of data needed for learning. The derivation is mathematically explicit and generalizes a known result. The simulations on the Nishimori line show that the formula correctly predicts the onset of learning for P=2 and P=3. This preempts the failure mode that the formula might only hold for P=2. The formula is a key quantitative result of the chapter.

nodes.title: Closed-form critical load for correlated patterns generalizes previous results

nodes.content: On the MNIST dataset with P=1000 hidden units, training the DAM with the effective loss (Eq. 4.12) using ς=0.25 achieves 96% classification accuracy, compared to 91% with standard training at β=18 and 79% at β=6 (Table 4.1). The memories learned with effective loss are visibly cleaner and more interpretable (Fig. 4.4 vs Fig. 4.3). This demonstrates a significant improvement in training stability and prototype quality.

metadata.credit: The empirical results show a clear and substantial improvement in accuracy and prototype quality on a standard benchmark. The comparison against multiple fixed β values shows that the improvement is not simply due to choosing a different β. This preempts the failure mode that the effective loss might not provide any practical benefit. The result underwrite the conclusion that the regularization inspired by the teacher-student analysis is effective for training DAMs.

nodes.title: Effective loss regularization achieves 96% accuracy on MNIST

nodes.content: For the DAM model, the paper provides an analytical proof (Appendix 4.I) that if a set of parameters is a fixed point of the saddle-point equations (Eqs. 4.10) for P hidden units, then the duplicated parameters (Eqs. 4.13) form a fixed point for P+R hidden units. Furthermore, for sufficiently large β, these duplicated fixed points are saddle points, not local minima. The proof uses the structure of the saddle-point equations and the properties of the softmax function.

metadata.credit: The proof establishes a rigorous mathematical principle that wider DAMs contain the stationary points of narrower DAMs as saddle points. This is a non-trivial result that goes beyond the generic embedding principle for neural networks. The proof is self-contained and does not rely on external citations. It provides the theoretical foundation for the splitting steepest descent algorithm. Without this proof, the algorithm would be heuristic.

nodes.title: Analytical proof of saddle-point hierarchy principle

nodes.content: On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, the splitting steepest descent algorithm (Alg. 1) reduces training time from linear in the maximum number of hidden units P_max to approximately logarithmic in P_max (Fig. 4.7), while maintaining comparable classification accuracy. For P_max=2000 on MNIST, the training time with splitting is about 5 times faster than without splitting. The speedup is consistent across multiple random seeds.

metadata.credit: The empirical results demonstrate a dramatic practical acceleration for training large DAMs. The comparison against standard training under controlled conditions (same accuracy, multiple seeds) shows that the speedup is robust. This preempts the failure mode that the algorithm might not provide significant speedup in practice. The result underwrite the conclusion that exploiting the saddle-point hierarchy can substantially reduce computational cost.

nodes.title: Splitting steepest descent reduces training time from linear to logarithmic

nodes.content: On MNIST, the DAM learns visually interpretable prototypes (memories) that resemble handwritten digits (Fig. 4.1, 4.4). Approximately 98% of test data points are classified into the class of the memory they most resemble (1-nearest neighbor fidelity). In unsupervised training on MNIST patches using minimum entropy regularization (Eq. 4.15), the DAM discovers latent classes that correspond to digit types (Fig. 4.5), demonstrating interpretability beyond supervised learning.

metadata.credit: The paper provides concrete visual evidence that the DAM learns meaningful prototypes, and the 1-NN fidelity metric quantifies the interpretability to some extent. The unsupervised result shows that the model can discover structure without labels, which is a strong indicator of interpretability. This preempts the failure mode that the model might only be interpretable in a supervised setting. The results underwrite the conclusion that the DAM is an interpretable model.

nodes.title: DAM learns interpretable prototypes in supervised and unsupervised settings

steps.reasoning: The paper studies a dense Hopfield network (dense HN) in the teacher-student setting. A teacher dense HN with a single planted pattern $\xi^* \in \{-1,1\}^N$ and hyperparameters $p^*$ (interaction order) and $\beta^*$ (inverse temperature) generates $M$ examples $\sigma^a$ from its Gibbs distribution. A student dense HN with hyperparameters $p$ and $\beta$ infers the teacher pattern by sampling from the posterior distribution $P(\xi|\sigma) \propto \exp(-\beta H[\xi|\sigma])$, where $H[\xi|\sigma]$ is the Hamiltonian with the examples acting as memories.

The paper considers the Nishimori line, where the student matches the teacher's hyperparameters: $p=p^*$ and $\beta=\beta^*$. On this line, the system is replica symmetric and the free entropy is given by Eq. (2.4) with saddle-point equations (2.5). The order parameters include $q^*$ (teacher-student overlap), $q$ (student-student overlap), and $m$ (student-example overlap).

The paper recalls the direct problem studied by Gardner: a dense HN with $M$ i.i.d. random memories $\xi^\mu$ has a spin-glass phase where $m=0$ (no retrieval) but $q>0$ (frozen states). The paramagnetic-to-spin-glass ($P$-$SG$) transition in the direct model is not captured accurately by the replica-symmetric approximation for $p \geq 3$, and 1RSB calculations suffer from numerical instability at large $p$.

The paper argues that on the Nishimori line, the inverse model's $gR$ (global retrieval) phase transition coincides with the exact $P$-$SG$ transition of the direct model. The argument proceeds in two directions. First, if the inverse model is in the paramagnetic phase, then the example distribution $P(\sigma)$ is contiguous to the uniform distribution (quiet planting), implying the direct model is also paramagnetic. This gives that the $gR$ transition temperature of the inverse model is at least as high as the $P$-$SG$ transition temperature of the direct model.

Second, if the direct model is in the paramagnetic phase, the paper shows that its average replicated partition function can be approximated in a form identical to that of the inverse model with $T > T_{\text{crit}}$, implying the inverse model is also paramagnetic. Therefore, the two transitions coincide.

The paper verifies this equivalence numerically by solving the saddle-point equations (2.5) on the Nishimori line for $p=3,4,10$ (Fig. 2.2). The $gR$ transition line matches the 1RSB $P$-$SG$ transition temperature $T_s(\alpha,p)$ of the direct model, obtained by rescaling results from the Gaussian spin-glass model. The metastable $lR$ phase coincides with the d1RSB phase.

The paper concludes that on the Nishimori line ($p=p^*$, $\beta=\beta^*$), the phase where the student learns the teacher pattern (the $gR$ phase) coincides with the spin-glass phase of the direct model. This refines the quiet planting bound by showing the learning phase extends exactly as far as the spin-glass phase, not just at least as far.

The paper studies the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks with mismatched interaction orders: the teacher has $p^*=2$ (original Hopfield model) and the student has $p \geq 3$ (even). The teacher's inverse temperature $\beta^*$ and the number of examples $M$ are scaled to make pattern inference possible.

The paper identifies two scaling regimes. In the large-noise scaling, $\beta^* \sim \mathcal{O}(N^{2/p-1})$ and $M \sim \mathcal{O}(N^{p-1})$, such that $\alpha = \frac{M p!}{N^{p-1}}$ and $\lambda = \frac{[\beta^*]^{p/2}}{(p/2)!} N^{p/2-1}$ are finite. In this regime, the teacher's examples are extremely noisy (uncorrelated with the teacher pattern), but the student can still learn.

The paper derives the free entropy for this mismatched case (Appendix 2.D). The saddle-point equations are similar to the matched case (Eqs. 2.5) but with $\beta^*$ replaced by $\lambda$. The student's effective inverse temperature is $\beta$, and the optimal performance occurs when $\beta = \lambda$.

The paper shows that for $p=4$, the student can tolerate teacher noise up to $\beta^* \sim \mathcal{O}(N^{1/2})$ (since $2/p-1 = -1/2$, so $\beta^* \sim N^{-1/2}$ means $T^* \sim N^{1/2}$). This requires $M \sim \mathcal{O}(N^3)$ examples. The phase diagram (Fig. 2.6, right panel) shows that for $\beta = \lambda$, the student enters the $gR$ phase at sufficiently large $\alpha$, achieving $q^* \approx 1$.

The paper also considers a finite-noise scaling where $\beta^* \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$ and $M \sim \mathcal{O}(N^{p/2})$, with $\alpha = \frac{M(p/2+1)!}{N^{p/2}}$ finite. In this regime, the saddle-point equations (2.6) are free from pattern interference, and the student can learn when $\beta$ matches the effective parameter $\eta$ (e.g., $\eta = \frac{2[\beta^*]^2}{(1-2\beta^*)^2}$ for $p=4$).

The paper concludes that a student with $p \geq 3$ can learn from a teacher with $p^*=2$ even when the teacher's inverse temperature $\beta^*$ is as low as $\mathcal{O}(N^{2/p-1})$, provided the student is shown enough examples $M \sim \mathcal{O}(N^{p-1})$. For $p=4$, this gives $\mathcal{O}(N^{1/2})$ noise tolerance. The student's performance is optimal when the effective inverse temperature $\lambda = \frac{[\beta^*]^{p/2}}{(p/2)!} N^{p/2-1}$ matches the student's inverse temperature $\beta$.

This conclusion builds on conclusion 2, which established that a student dense Hopfield network with $p \geq 3$ can learn from a teacher with $p^*=2$ in the finite-noise scaling regime, where $\beta^* \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$ and $M \sim \mathcal{O}(N^{p/2})$, with $\alpha = \frac{M(p/2+1)!}{N^{p/2}}$ finite. The saddle-point equations for this case are given by Eqs. (2.6), which do not involve the pattern interference term $\sqrt{\alpha r} x$.

The paper considers the zero-temperature limit ($\beta = \infty$) for the student. In this limit, the saddle-point equations (2.6) indicate that the student converges to one of the signal retrieval phases if and only if $k < \eta \alpha r^*$, where $k$ and $r^*$ are order parameters related to the student's overlap with examples and teacher pattern, respectively.

The paper models an adversarial attack: the student's initial pattern $\xi$ is corrupted by replacing a fraction $\varepsilon$ of its entries with those of a typical example $\sigma^a$. The initial conditions are sampled from $(1-\varepsilon)\delta(\xi_i - \xi_i^*) + \varepsilon \delta(\xi_i - \sigma_i^a)$.

Using the law of large numbers, the paper computes the initial values of $r^*$ and $k$:
$$
r^* \approx p(1-\varepsilon)^{p-1}, \quad k \approx p\varepsilon^{p-1}.
$$
These follow from the fact that the overlap between $\xi^*$ and $\sigma^a$ is approximately 0 for a typical example.

Substituting into the condition $k < \eta \alpha r^*$ gives:
$$
\varepsilon^{p-1} < \eta \alpha (1-\varepsilon)^{p-1} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \varepsilon < \frac{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}}{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}+1}.
$$
Thus, the largest adversarial perturbation $\varepsilon^*$ that still allows retrieval of the teacher pattern is $\varepsilon^* = \frac{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}}{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}+1}$.

The paper specifies $\eta$ for $p=4$: $\eta = \frac{2[\beta^*]^2}{(1-2\beta^*)^2}$. The formula shows that $\varepsilon^*$ increases monotonically with $\alpha$, meaning larger datasets improve adversarial robustness.

The paper verifies this formula with Monte Carlo simulations for $p=4$, $\beta^* = 1-1/\sqrt{2}$ (so $\eta=1$), and $\beta=\infty$ (Fig. 2.8). The analytical curve $\varepsilon^* = \alpha^{1/3}/(\alpha^{1/3}+1)$ matches the simulation data well.

The paper concludes that for a student dense Hopfield network with $p^*=2$, $p \geq 3$ (even), and zero temperature, the largest adversarial perturbation that still allows retrieval of the teacher pattern is given by $\varepsilon^* = \frac{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}}{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}+1}$, where $\alpha$ is the finite-noise load and $\eta$ depends on $\beta^*$ and $p$. This formula shows that adversarial robustness increases monotonically with the dataset size $\alpha$.

This conclusion builds on conclusions 1 and 2. Conclusion 1 established the equivalence of the learning phase ($gR$) on the Nishimori line with the spin-glass phase of the direct model. Conclusion 2 established that with mismatched interaction orders ($p^*=2$, $p \geq 3$), the student can have extensive noise tolerance, and the phase diagram includes an inaccurate example retrieval ($eR$) phase where the student has finite overlap with a noisy example but zero overlap with the teacher pattern.

The paper recalls that Krotov and Hopfield observed that dense Hopfield networks are adversarially robust in the prototype regime but vulnerable in the feature regime. The teacher-student setting provides a controlled framework to understand this behavior through the phase structure.

The paper explains that in the accurate $eR$ phase (which occurs when $T^* < T_{\text{crit}}$), the examples are strongly correlated with the teacher pattern. Retrieving an example is equivalent to recovering the signal, so this phase is inherently robust to adversarial attacks.

In the $gR$ phase (feature regime), the student learns the teacher pattern from weakly correlated examples. However, when the $gR$ phase overlaps with the inaccurate $eR$ phase (where the student has finite overlap with a noisy example but zero overlap with the teacher pattern), the student can be vulnerable to adversarial attacks that push it into the inaccurate $eR$ phase.

The paper shows that increasing the dataset size $\alpha$ stabilizes the $gR$ phase (as seen from the formula $\varepsilon^* = [\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}/([\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}+1)$ in conclusion 3), which increases robustness. This explains why larger neural networks are often more adversarially robust.

The paper concludes that the adversarial robustness of dense Hopfield networks changes with the interaction order $p$ because the prototype phase ($eR$) is inherently robust, while the feature phase ($gR$) can be vulnerable when it overlaps with the inaccurate $eR$ phase. Increasing the dataset size $\alpha$ stabilizes the $gR$ phase and increases robustness.

The paper argues that this teacher-student setting with uncorrelated patterns and $P > P^*$ can serve as a toy model for the lottery ticket hypothesis. The lottery ticket hypothesis states that overparameterized neural networks contain subnetworks (winning tickets) that, when trained in isolation, achieve comparable accuracy and converge faster.

The paper performs a numerical experiment (Section 3.3.2.3): a teacher with $P^*=4$ i.i.d. Gaussian patterns generates data. A student (student 0) with $P=8$ i.i.d. Gaussian patterns is trained. After training, the Euclidean norms of the learned patterns are computed.

A variant of magnitude pruning is applied: the $P^*=4$ patterns of student 0 with the largest Euclidean norms are selected as the initial conditions for a new student (student B) with $P=4$ patterns. A control student (student A) is initialized with $P=4$ i.i.d. Gaussian patterns.

Both student A and student B are trained on the same data. The magnetization $m$ is recorded as a function of training epochs. The results (Fig. 3.7) show that student B initially converges more quickly than student A, i.e., $m_B > m_A$ at early epochs. The lead of student B diminishes over time due to ergodicity.

The paper concludes that the teacher-student setting with uncorrelated patterns and $P > P^*$ can serve as a toy model for the lottery ticket hypothesis. Magnitude pruning identifies a winning ticket (student B) that converges faster when retrained from its initial conditions compared to a randomly initialized network of the same size. The lead of the winning ticket diminishes over time due to ergodicity.

The paper introduces a dense associative memory (DAM) model derived from a Boltzmann machine with three layers: data layer $\mathbf{x}$ (von Mises-Fisher distribution), hidden layer $\mathbf{h}$ (categorical), and class layer $\mathbf{q}$ (categorical). The marginal distribution of the visible layer $(\mathbf{x}, y)$ is given by Eq. (4.3): $\mathrm{P}_\beta(\mathbf{x}, y|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{\mu=1}^P p_y^\mu \frac{\exp(\beta \sum_i w_i^\mu x_i)}{\Omega_N(\beta)} + p_y^0 \frac{1}{\Omega_N(0)}$.

The paper also studies the teacher-student setting for this DAM. A teacher DAM generates $M$ examples $\mathcal{D} = \{\mathbf{x}^c, y^c\}$, and a student DAM samples its weights from the posterior distribution (Eq. 4.5). Using the replica method, the paper derives the free entropy (Eq. 4.26) and the saddle-point equations (Eqs. 4.10) for the expected teacher-student overlaps $m^{\mu_*\mu}$ and class weights $p_y^\gamma$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
m^{\mu_*\mu} &= \varsigma\left(2\beta_{\text{eff}}\varrho \sqrt{\sum_i [\bar{x}_i^\mu]^2}\right) \frac{\sum_i x_i^{*\mu_*} \bar{x}_i^\mu}{\sqrt{\sum_i [\bar{x}_i^\mu]^2}} \\
p_y^\gamma &= \frac{\bar{p}_y^\gamma}{\zeta_y^\gamma(\overline{\mathbf{p}}; p_{\mathbf{h}})} \\
\bar{x}_i^\mu &= \sum_{\mu_*=1}^{P^*} x_i^{*\mu_*} \sum_{y=0}^C q_y^{*\mu_*} \sigma_\mu(\beta_{\text{eff}} m^{\mu_*} + \log[\mathbf{p}_y]) \\
\bar{p}_y^\gamma &= \sum_{\mu_*=1}^{P^*} q_y^{*\mu_*} \sigma_\gamma(\beta_{\text{eff}} m^{\mu_*} + \log[\mathbf{p}_y])
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\beta_{\text{eff}} = \varsigma(2v)\beta$, $v = \beta^*/N$, $\varrho = M/(P^*N)$, and $\varsigma(x) = x/(\sqrt{x^2+1}+1)$.

The paper shows that in the limit of large data ($\varrho \to \infty$) and low teacher noise ($v \to \infty$), the teacher-student saddle-point equations reduce to the maximum likelihood stationary conditions (Eqs. 4.6). Specifically, as $\varrho \to \infty$, $\varsigma(2\beta_{\text{eff}}\varrho \sqrt{\sum_i [\bar{x}_i^\mu]^2}) \to 1$, and as $v \to \infty$, $\beta_{\text{eff}} \to \beta$. Thus, the fixed points of the posterior sampling coincide with the stationary points of the loss.

The paper concludes that the stationary points of the negative log-likelihood loss for the DAM satisfy self-consistent equations (Eqs. 4.6), and in the teacher-student setting, the fixed points of posterior sampling satisfy analogous saddle-point equations (Eqs. 4.10). In the limit of large data and low teacher noise, the two frameworks are equivalent.
