This conclusion builds on conclusion 11, which established the equivalence between the teacher-student saddle-point equations and the maximum likelihood stationary conditions in the limit of large data and low teacher noise. The teacher-student analysis revealed that the effective inverse temperature should be $\beta_{\text{eff}} = \varsigma\beta$ with $\varsigma < 1$ when the teacher has finite noise.

The paper proposes to train the DAM by minimizing the effective loss $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{p}) = -\frac{1}{P^*} \sum_{\mu=1}^{P^*} \sum_{y=0}^C q_y^{*\mu} \log \mathcal{P}_{\beta,\varsigma}(\mathbf{x}^{*\mu}, y|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{p})$ (Eq. 4.12), where $\mathcal{P}_{\beta,\varsigma}$ has effective inverse temperature $\varsigma\beta$ in the exponential argument. The parameter $\varsigma$ mimics the noise present in the data generation process.

The paper trains DAMs on MNIST with $P=1000$ hidden units using standard training (Eq. 4.4) at various $\beta$ values, and using the effective loss with $\varsigma=0.25$. Standard training at $\beta=18$ achieves 91% accuracy, at $\beta=6$ achieves 79% accuracy. Training with the effective loss achieves 96% accuracy (Table 4.1).

The paper shows that the effective loss training produces cleaner memories (Fig. 4.4, top panel) compared to standard training (Fig. 4.3). The regularization parameter $\varsigma$ slows down the evolution of $\beta$ enough to let the DAM learn much cleaner memories.

The paper concludes that training a DAM by minimizing the effective loss with a regularization parameter $\varsigma < 1$ significantly improves training stability and classification accuracy. On MNIST, this method achieves 96% accuracy with $P=1000$ hidden units, compared to 91% with standard training at $\beta=18$ and 79% at $\beta=6$. The parameter $\varsigma$ mimics the noise present in the data generation process.

This conclusion builds on conclusion 11, which derived the saddle-point equations (Eqs. 4.10) for the DAM in the teacher-student setting. The paper now studies the structure of fixed points of these equations.

The paper shows (Appendix 4.I) that if a set of parameters $\bar{x}_i^{\text{fixed},\mu}$, $\bar{p}_y^{\text{fixed},\gamma}$, $m^{\text{fixed},\mu_*\gamma}$, $p_y^{\text{fixed},\gamma}$ with hidden unit prior $p_{\mathbf{h}}^{\text{given}}(\gamma)$ is a fixed point of Eqs. (4.10) for a DAM with $P$ hidden units, then the duplicated parameters (Eqs. 4.13) form a fixed point for a DAM with $P+R$ hidden units (where $R \leq P$). The duplication involves copying some of the hidden units and rescaling the class weights and priors accordingly.

The paper analyzes the stability of this duplicated fixed point. For sufficiently large $\beta$, the Jacobian of the saddle-point equations has eigenvalues with magnitude greater than 1 in directions that break the permutation symmetry between a hidden unit and its duplicate. This is shown by computing the quadratic form of the Jacobian in the direction $\mathbf{v}$ that is antisymmetric between the original and duplicate units (Appendix 4.I).

The paper concludes that for sufficiently large $\beta$, the duplicated fixed point is a saddle point, not a local minimum. This establishes that wider DAMs contain the stationary points of narrower DAMs as saddle points, a property called the saddle-point hierarchy principle.
Section 4.3.2; Appendix 4.I

This conclusion builds on conclusion 13, which established the saddle-point hierarchy principle: wider DAMs contain the stationary points of narrower DAMs as saddle points. This suggests that one can start with a small DAM and grow it during training.

The paper implements the splitting steepest descent algorithm (Alg. 1) for the DAM. The algorithm starts with a small number of hidden units $P_{\text{cur}}$, trains the DAM, then repeatedly duplicates some hidden units (splits), escapes the saddle point via second-order descent, and continues training. The splitting is guided by the eigenvectors of the splitting matrices $\mathcal{S}_\mu$ (Appendix 4.K).

The paper trains DAMs on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST with and without splitting, comparing training time and classification accuracy as a function of the maximum number of hidden units $P_{\text{max}}$ (Fig. 4.7). Without splitting, training time is proportional to $P_{\text{max}}$. With splitting, training time is approximately logarithmic in $P_{\text{max}}$ (piecewise constant, increasing only when the number of while-loop iterations increases).
The classification accuracy is comparable with and without splitting. For MNIST, splitting does not significantly affect accuracy; for Fashion-MNIST, splitting slightly improves accuracy.

The paper concludes that implementing the splitting steepest descent algorithm that exploits the saddle-point hierarchy reduces training time from linear in $P_{\text{max}}$ to approximately logarithmic in $P_{\text{max}}$. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, DAMs trained with splitting achieve comparable classification accuracy to those trained without splitting, but with significantly reduced computational cost, especially for large $P_{\text{max}}$.

The paper trains the DAM model on the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits using constrained stochastic gradient descent of the negative log-likelihood loss (Eq. 4.4) with regularization (effective loss Eq. 4.12). The learned memories $\mathbf{w}^\mu$ are interpretable prototypes (Fig. 4.1, 4.4).

The paper shows that each memory $\mathbf{w}^\mu$ is associated with a soft label $\mathbf{p}^\mu/p_{\mathbf{h}}(\mu)$ that corresponds to a digit class (Fig. 4.4, bottom panel). The column-wise maxima of the rescaled class weights indicate the class of each memory.

The paper measures the 1-nearest neighbor fidelity: approximately 98% of test data points are classified into the class of the memory they most resemble. This fidelity is higher for correctly classified points (99%) than for incorrectly classified points (70%).

The paper also demonstrates unsupervised classification using a minimum entropy regularization (Eq. 4.15). The DAM is trained on $6\times6$ patches of MNIST digits without labels, assuming $C=10$ latent classes. The learned class weights $\mathbf{p}^\mu/p_{\mathbf{h}}(\mu)$ discover latent classes corresponding to digit types (Fig. 4.5, 4.8-4.11).

The paper concludes that the DAM model learns interpretable prototypes in both supervised and unsupervised settings. In supervised training, each memory is associated with a soft label corresponding to a digit class, and the model achieves high 1-nearest neighbor fidelity. In unsupervised training, the DAM discovers latent classes that correspond to digit types.

open_questions.content: Several scientifically meaningful unresolved issues remain after this work. In the context of dense Hopfield networks (Chapter 2), it would be interesting to see if exponential interaction models can achieve $\mathcal{O}(N)$ noise tolerance at the cost of an exponential number of training examples, and to study exponential models in the teacher-student setting. The current model uses a teacher with only one pattern; to describe adversarial attacks aiming to misclassify data, a teacher with at least two patterns is needed, which could be studied using an approach similar to that for RBMs with multiple hidden units. It remains to be investigated whether the independence of performance on the number of patterns observed in RBMs also holds for $p$-body dense networks. For restricted Boltzmann machines (Chapter 3), one could study the learning dynamics of the magnitude pruning experiment to gain additional insight into the lottery ticket hypothesis, or characterize the distribution of winning ticket initial conditions. Extending the study to the case where $P$ and $P^*$ are of order $N$ would be relevant for real-world RBMs with many hidden units. Introducing correlations between the columns of the teacher's weight matrix (low-rank SVD structure) in addition to correlations between patterns would allow the teacher to generate even more structured data, and could be used to investigate whether the distinction between $\text{PSB}_s$ and $\text{PSB}_t$ persists in real data and affects critical slowing down. Other generative models with finite hidden units, such as modern Hopfield networks, could also be studied in the teacher-student setting. For the dense associative memory model (Chapter 4), further research is needed to determine the asymptotic functional form of the training time with splitting steepest descent. Studying the teacher-student setting with teacher inverse temperature $\beta^*$ less than order $N$ is another interesting direction. The tradeoff between splitting steepest descent and random noise methods for breaking permutation symmetry should be investigated. More generally, one could study how permutation symmetry breaking takes place in related energy models such as attentional Boltzmann machines, and investigate whether there are similarities between cellular division and splitting steepest descent. Finally, it would be interesting to see if splitting steepest descent and the proposed regularization technique can improve the training of transformers and generative diffusion models.
